claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a heterogeneous native oxide and defect distribution.
Gentle polishing followed by thermal annealing in a controlled atmosphere will produce a more continuous, chemically stable, and defect-reduced oxide film on Q235 steel.
The treated oxide film will act as a barrier to corrosive attack.
Increasing oxide-film continuity and stability will reduce the number of active corrosion sites and suppress localized anodic dissolution.
The improved oxide barrier will limit chloride-ion ingress.
Limiting chloride ingress and localized dissolution will reduce the formation of microcracks and pits that promote corrosion propagation.
Surface-treated Q235 steel will exhibit suppressed corrosion initiation and degradation relative to untreated Q235 steel in chloride-rich media at approximately 25°C and 70–90°C.
Treated samples will have lower corrosion current density than untreated samples after equivalent chloride exposure.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy can characterize passive-film behavior.
Corrosion current density will be measured via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
Treated samples will exhibit less corrosion-related weight loss than untreated samples.
Treated samples will exhibit fewer or less-developed corrosion cracks and pits than untreated samples.
Temperature-dependent thermal stress can influence cracking behavior.
Very high chloride concentrations, very high temperatures, or additional mechanical stresses may overwhelm the protective oxide layer.
Residual stress and inherent defect distributions may significantly influence Q235 corrosion behavior.
The durability and uniformity of corrosion suppression may differ under long-term real-world exposure.
A controlled comparison will use treated and as-received Q235 batches exposed to identical 3.5 wt% NaCl solutions at approximately 25°C and 70–90°C for fixed durations.

Failure of treated samples to show statistically significant reductions in corrosion current density, weight loss, and crack or pit density relative to untreated controls will falsify the proposed protective-oxide hypothesis.
